audit_result.proof_trace: Three user-facing OAuth tables (`oauth.applications`, `oauth.authorization_codes`, `oauth.user_consents`) set only `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` but not `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, leaving the table owner exempt from RLS policies. The member and attendance schemas were explicitly patched with FORCE RLS in `20260317000001_fix_security_permissions.sql` (lines 28–32, 93–96) with the stated goal of preventing accidental owner-level bypass, but the later-added oauth schema omits this hardening. Practical exploitability is limited to table-owner-level code paths (e.g., SECURITY DEFINER functions), since the `postgres` superuser and `service_role` (BYPASSRLS) already bypass RLS regardless.
audit_result.attack_scenario: A SECURITY DEFINER function created in the oauth schema (e.g., the existing `oauth.cleanup_expired_codes()`) executes as its definer with table-owner privileges, bypassing the `USING(false)` policy on `oauth.authorization_codes`; a malicious or compromised function added to this schema could read or forge active authorization codes without passing any RLS policy.

PROP-kintai-v3-st-inv-010.text: RLS FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY must be enabled on all user-facing tables.
PROP-kintai-v3-st-inv-010.assertion: forall table in user_tables: ALTER TABLE table FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY == enabled
